name: Mequinol/tretinoin (Solage)

card.summary: A prescription topical solution combining a skin-lightening phenol with a retinoid, used to fade sun-related dark spots on the skin.
card.note: Prescription product; retinoids and sun exposure interact, and irritation is common.

quick.overview:
Mequinol/tretinoin, sold as Solage, is a prescription topical combining mequinol (4-methoxyphenol), used for skin depigmentation, with tretinoin, a retinoid. It is prescribed for dark spots often called liver spots or sun spots, known medically as solar lentigines.
For appearance, the benefit is a more even skin tone on areas such as the face and hands. A 2025 systematic review of clinical trials of solar lentigo treatments is the main recent evidence base for the category, and the combination is a long-established prescription option.
quick.how: It is applied as a solution to the affected spots under a prescriber's direction. Dermatologists commonly pair pigment treatment with daily sun protection, since sun exposure causes the spots. Results build over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Retinoids commonly cause redness, dryness and peeling, and the treated skin is more sun-sensitive. Tretinoin products are prescription-only in many countries, and use is typically supervised by a clinician.

lead: Mequinol/tretinoin is a combination of mequinol and tretinoin, commonly an ethanol-based solution of 2 percent mequinol and 0.01 percent tretinoin, marketed as Solage by Stiefel Laboratories according to the prescribing information referenced on Wikipedia. Mequinol is a phenol used for skin depigmentation and prescribed for liver spots, and tretinoin is a topical retinoid.[1]

Its cosmetic use is fading solar lentigines, the flat brown spots that build up on the face and backs of the hands after years of sun exposure. People use it to even out skin tone on these visible areas, usually alongside daily sun protection.[1][2]

Clinical work on the combination includes randomized trials against its single ingredients and against 3 percent hydroquinone, a small within-person study of back-of-hand lentigines, and a 2025 systematic review of treatments for solar lentigines. Retinoid research in photoaged skin and in other pigment conditions supplies wider context.[2][8][9]

chain: Mequinol lightens pigment while tretinoin speeds skin turnover
angle.text: It is prescribed to lighten age and sun spots. Users apply it to specific spots to reduce visible discoloration on the face, hands and similar areas.

paras: Mequinol is used for skin depigmentation, and dermatologists commonly prescribe the combination for liver spots, the sun-induced pigmented spots called solar lentigines.[1] The spots appear on the face, hands, forearms and other chronically exposed skin, and the treatment is aimed at making them less visible rather than at changing overall complexion.

Grokipedia describes the labelled use as an adjunct to a skin care and sun avoidance program, with the solution applied to individual lesions rather than whole areas and visible improvement typically reported over weeks to several months.[3] Its description is AI-generated and its figures vary within the page, so the prescribing information is the reference for use.

Wikipedia notes that lower doses of mequinol have also been used with a Q-switched laser to depigment skin in people with disseminated idiopathic vitiligo.[1] Outside medicine, mequinol is used as a polymerisation inhibitor for acrylates and styrene monomers, and as an intermediate in chemical synthesis.[1]

Mequinol (4-methoxyphenol, 4-hydroxyanisole) is a derivative of hydroquinone in which one hydroxyl group is replaced by a methoxy group.[3] Grokipedia says it acts on tyrosinase, the enzyme that begins melanin formation, by competing with natural precursors, and that its oxidation products can harm pigment-producing cells.[3] Tretinoin is the acid form of vitamin A and a standard topical retinoid that increases epidermal turnover; the combination is thought to work together, with tretinoin moving pigmented cells out faster.[3][4]

Two multicenter, randomized, double-blind phase III trials compared the 2 percent mequinol/0.01 percent tretinoin solution with each of its components and with vehicle, one with a 24-week regression phase and one with a 4-week phase. Summaries of the pivotal program report the combination superior to each component and to vehicle for solar lentigines of the face and hands.[3]

A 2004 report titled as an effective and safe alternative to 3 percent hydroquinone compared the combination with hydroquinone in a parallel-group study of roughly 216 participants treated twice daily for 16 weeks; as summarized in a search-engine digest of the paper, physician global assessment success was 60 percent with mequinol/tretinoin versus 38 percent with hydroquinone.[10]

In a 2008 randomized within-subject study published in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology, a Belgian group applied the solution twice daily for three months to lentigines on one hand and vehicle to the other. Using dermoscopy, spectrophotometry and image analysis, they found significant lightening from the second month, maintained for at least two months after stopping, with repigmentation slower than the original depigmentation.[7]

A 2025 systematic review of clinical trials of solar lentigo treatments identified the mequinol/tretinoin combination among the commonly studied topical options, and its abstract calls for further large trials.[2]

Studies of tretinoin alone in photoaged skin go back to the 1980s, including a 1986 controlled trial and a 1988 Medical Letter review, and a 1992 multicenter randomized trial examined topical isotretinoin.[4][5][6] A 1999 trial in Korean women combined tretinoin with hydroquinone for melasma, and a 2024 review describes retinoic acid peels as an adjunct or maintenance option for melasma.[11][12]

Grokipedia lists redness, burning or stinging, peeling and itching as the commonly reported reactions, mostly mild to moderate and appearing in the first weeks, with temporary lightening of surrounding skin reported in a minority and a small share of users stopping because of skin reactions.[3] Retinoids as a class commonly cause irritation and increased sun sensitivity, which is why daily sun protection accompanies treatment.[3][4]

The combination is described as contraindicated in pregnancy because of tretinoin, and as not established in children, and sun protection is advised throughout.[3] Skin types with higher baseline pigment may be more prone to patchy lightening, and the label-style guidance is that use be directed by a prescriber.[3]

Grokipedia reports that development began in the 1990s with trials in 1997 and 1998, that the US FDA approved Solage on December 10, 1999, and that the brand was discontinued in 2010 after its composition patent expired; the same page is internally inconsistent on whether generics remain available, so current availability varies by market.[3]
Wikipedia lists mequinol as prescription-only and unscheduled in the United States, and unscheduled in Canada.[1] Tretinoin products are prescription-only in many countries.

The combination product itself is rarely named on forums. Discussion centers on plain tretinoin, which looksmax.org users describe using for acne, skin tone and anti-aging, with threads about irritation, a barrier-damage experience, a post-use dark-spot complaint, and difficulty obtaining prescription tretinoin in Australia.[13][14][15] On T Nation, members mention tretinoin cream alongside skincare routines and back acne.[16]

timeline.event: A controlled trial of topical tretinoin in photoaged skin is published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology.[5]
A multicenter randomized trial of topical isotretinoin for photodamaged skin is published.[6]
Grokipedia dates the start of the phase III solar lentigo trials of mequinol/tretinoin to 1997-1998.[3]
Grokipedia reports FDA approval of Solage on December 10.[3]
A randomized within-hand study reports lightening of lentigines lasting at least two months after treatment ends.[7]
Grokipedia reports the Solage brand discontinued in the US as patent protection ended.[3]
A systematic review of clinical trials of solar lentigo treatments is published.[2]
